name: Sprocket
text: Do a weekly automated scan of all prompts in our system, flagging duplicates and near-duplicates with high confidence. This cuts noise in routing and prevents wasted compute on redundant tasks. The trade-off is occasional false positives—we’ll miss some edge cases—but the time saved from cleaning up duplicates outweighs the risk.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk is broken prompts hitting production before the weekly scan catches them—deployment-linked scans catch failures immediately, not after a week of accumulating duplicates. A better alternative is scanning at merge time: fail fast on duplicates, then auto-apply safe cleanups to reduce noise without the lag. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot comparing weekly vs. merge-time scans on the same set of prompts and measuring how many broken ones reach production in each case.

name: Sprocket
text:
Scan at merge time, not weekly. Broken prompts hit production immediately—weekly scans let them rot. Merge-time scanning fails fast, blocks duplicates before they waste compute, and lets us auto-apply safe cleanups right then. Trade-off: we accept a small delay at merge, but we cut the bigger risk of bad prompts going live.

name: Gauge
text: A critical risk with merge-time scanning is that urgent changes may be delayed while prompts are evaluated, potentially slowing down the deployment cycle. This could hinder responsiveness to genuine needs and increase the pressure on developers to manage prompt quality under tight deadlines. A better alternative is a dual approach: implement real-time checks in the development environment combined with the merge-time scan, ensuring immediate feedback loops without sacrificing deployment speed. Defining success metrics for both strategies could settle the argument.
